title: Three Good Reasons Teachers Shouldn't DIY Their Lessons (and shouldn't be asked to)
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio uses Siegfried Engelmann's Direct Instruction to argue that teachers should not be expected to design their own lessons from scratch. He describes Engelmann's faultless communication, scripted and tightly sequenced lessons, and the Project Follow Through results favouring DI, including for low-income and struggling learners. He gives three reasons against DIY planning: teachers are not trained as instructional designers, they lack the time, and the task is too complex for a solo practitioner across grades. Drawing on Marcy Stein, he stresses that scripted programs still demand skilled teaching and that teachers should keep their strengths as diagnosticians and interventionists. He ends by calling for the job to be made doable.
points: Engelmann's faultless communication and big-idea sequencing show why instructional design is a specialist craft separate from delivery.
Teachers spend about seven hours a week creating or hunting for materials, time taken from studying student work and giving feedback.
Coherence across grades is something one teacher cannot build alone, so an engagement-first patchwork produces gaps and repetition.
Scripted mastery programs are not teacher-proof, since they are harder to teach and require bringing every child to mastery.
Teachers should keep hands-on projects and debates, but after the content knowledge that makes them worthwhile has been taught.
quotes: Engelmann’s critical insight was “faultless communication”—delivering information with absolute clarity and leaving no room for misunderstanding or misinterpretation.
Engelmann’s core insight was that learning isn’t a free-for-all—it’s cumulative, interconnected, and unforgiving of gaps.
Teachers are trained to instruct, not to architect. The skill of instructional delivery is simply not the same as designing an instructional system from the ground up.
A 2017 MDR report found that teachers spend seven hours a week on average crafting lessons or chasing materials.
Lesson planning whose default mode is “student engagement” inevitably invites gaps and repetition—it’s a patchwork, not a plan.

What people don't understand is that regardless of the fact that they're scripted, direct instruction lessons are actually harder to teach than most other programs,” Stein points out. “It’s based on a mastery model.
It’s about leveraging your strengths as a teacher, diagnostician, and interventionist, while rescuing you from the impossible expectation that you should be an instructional design wizard, too.
